Payment
PAY-ment
n. (the act of paying; the discharge of a debt or obligation by giving what is due)
Old French paiement, from payer, to pay, from Latin pacare, to pacify or satisfy, itself from pax, peace. A payment is, at its Latin root, whatever it takes to make a matter peaceable again between debtor and creditor.

Biblical Definition

Christ's parable of the unmerciful servant turns entirely on a payment that cannot possibly be made. A servant owing ten thousand talents, an amount no ordinary laborer could repay across many lifetimes, stands before his king with no defense: forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made. The sentence is severe and, by the ordinary logic of debt, entirely just — a debt this size demands the only payment left available once money has run out, the debtor's own person and household sold to recover what can be recovered.

What makes the parable devastating is what happens next: the servant falls down and worships his lord, and the lord, moved with compassion, forgives him the whole debt outright, releasing him from a payment that was never actually going to be made even by the sale of everything he owned. Christ's whole point in the parable turns on what that same forgiven servant then does to a fellow servant who owes him a debt smaller by a factor of many thousands, refusing him the same mercy he had just been shown. Payment, in this parable, is not merely a financial transaction; it is the exact axis on which Christ measures whether a man who has received an impossible debt's forgiveness has understood anything at all about what he was given.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the act of paying; the discharge of a debt, or the fulfillment of an obligation, by giving money or its equivalent.

expand to see more

PAYMENT, n. The act of paying; the discharge of an obligation by delivering money or its value.

TALENT, n. An ancient unit of weight and money, among the largest in Scripture, representing great value.

DEBT, n. That which is owed by one person to another; an obligation to pay or perform.

COMPASSION, n. A feeling of sorrow or pity for the sufferings of another, moving one to relieve them.

FORGIVE, v.t. To pardon; to give up resentment or claim for compensation; to remit a debt or offense.

Key Scripture

Mat 18:23 — "Therefore is the kingdom of heaven likened unto a certain king, which would take account of his servants."

Mat 18:24 — "And when he had begun to reckon, one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents."

Mat 18:25 — "But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made."

Mat 18:27 — "Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt."

Modern Corruption

Forgiveness is treated as the automatic erasure of a debt too small to matter, when Christ's parable is built entirely on a debt so large that payment was structurally impossible, making the king's forgiveness costly rather than casual.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; payment still means the discharge of a debt. The principle worth recovering is the deliberate scale Christ builds into the parable. Ten thousand talents was not a debt a servant could plausibly have accumulated through ordinary means, and the payment commanded, the sale of his wife, children, and all he had, would not have come close to satisfying it either — the debt was, by design, beyond any payment the servant himself could ever supply.

The forgiven servant's subsequent refusal to extend even a fraction of that same mercy to a debtor who owed him a comparatively trivial sum is what exposes the whole point of the parable: a man who has genuinely understood what it cost to have an impossible payment cancelled cannot turn around and demand a payable one from someone else without revealing that he never understood the gift at all. Christ's warning that follows, of the unmerciful servant delivered to the tormentors, ties the doctrine of forgiveness directly to whether a forgiven debtor forgives in turn.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apodidomi (G591), to give back, to pay off, to render what is due; the verb behind “to pay” and “payment” throughout the parable of Matthew 18.

expand to see more

Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to pay off, to render fully; the verb underlying both “to pay” and “payment” in Matthew 18:25-28.

Greek talanton (G5007) — a talent, the largest unit of currency in the New Testament, used here to signal a debt beyond ordinary repayment.

Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, to be indebted; the standing verb for the servant's obligation.

Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion, literally in the bowels; the king's response that cancels the payment altogether.

Greek aphiemi (G863) — to send away, to forgive, to release from obligation; the verb behind “forgave him the debt” in Matthew 18:27.

Usage

"“he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold... and payment to be made” — the debt's demanded, impossible price."

"“moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt” — the payment cancelled outright."

"“one was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents” — the scale that makes the forgiveness costly, not casual."
